description: Exact integer arithmetic is unbounded in the Wolfram Language, which makes it a strong environment for number theory and combinatorics. This category covers primes and factorization, modular arithmetic, continued fractions, partition and counting functions, the combinatorial generators, the discrete delta and step functions, and bitwise operations on integers.

tools.name: Prime
tools.description: Gives the n-th prime number, with Prime[1] == 2. It uses fast prime counting and sieving internally, so even Prime[10^9] is feasible. It is Listable, so Prime[Range[10]] returns the first ten primes.
tools.notes: For a contiguous run of primes above a bound, NextPrime iterated is faster than computing PrimePi and then indexing.

tools.name: PrimeQ
tools.description: Tests whether an integer is prime, using a combination of strong pseudoprime tests (Miller-Rabin base 2 and 3 plus a Lucas test) that has no known counterexample. It is extremely fast even for numbers with hundreds of digits. The option GaussianIntegers -> True tests primality in the Gaussian integers.
tools.example:
PrimeQ[97]
PrimeQ[2^31 - 1]
Select[Range[50], PrimeQ]
PrimeQ[1 + 2 I, GaussianIntegers -> True]
tools.notes: PrimeQ is a probabilistic-style test in principle; for a certified proof use ProvablePrimeQ, which returns a primality certificate.

tools.name: NextPrime
tools.description: Gives the smallest prime greater than a number, with NextPrime[x, k] giving the k-th prime after it and negative k searching downward. PreviousPrime is the equivalent going down. These are the practical tools for finding primes near a target size, for example when generating cryptographic parameters.

tools.name: PrimePi
tools.description: Gives the number of primes less than or equal to x, the prime counting function pi(x). It uses an analytic combinatorial algorithm rather than sieving, so it handles arguments far beyond the range where listing primes is possible. It is the inverse companion of Prime.

tools.name: FactorInteger
tools.description: Gives the prime factorization of an integer as a list of {prime, exponent} pairs. Negative numbers include a {-1, 1} entry and rationals give negative exponents for denominator factors. The GaussianIntegers option factors over the Gaussian integers, and a second argument limits the amount of work spent on hard factors.
tools.usage:
FactorInteger[n]
FactorInteger[n, k]
FactorInteger[n, GaussianIntegers -> True]
tools.example:
FactorInteger[360]
FactorInteger[2^64 + 1]
FactorInteger[1/12]
Times @@ (#1^#2 & @@@ FactorInteger[360])
FactorInteger[5, GaussianIntegers -> True]
tools.notes: Factoring large semiprimes is computationally hard; FactorInteger may run for a very long time on numbers with two large prime factors.

tools.name: Divisors
tools.description: Gives the sorted list of all positive divisors of an integer, including 1 and the number itself. It works for Gaussian integers and for polynomials with the appropriate options. Use DivisorSum to sum a function over divisors without building the list.
tools.notes: The number of divisors is DivisorSigma[0, n] and their sum is DivisorSigma[1, n], both computed from the factorization without enumeration.

tools.name: DivisorSigma
tools.description: Gives the divisor function sigma_k(n), the sum of the k-th powers of the divisors of n. DivisorSigma[0, n] counts the divisors and DivisorSigma[1, n] sums them, which characterizes perfect and amicable numbers. It is computed from the prime factorization, so it is fast even for large n.

tools.name: EulerPhi
tools.description: Euler's totient function: the count of integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n. It gives the order of the multiplicative group modulo n, which is the exponent used in RSA and in Euler's theorem. It is computed directly from the factorization.
tools.notes: CarmichaelLambda gives the exponent of the group, which is at most EulerPhi[n] and is the tighter exponent for modular order computations.

tools.name: MoebiusMu
tools.description: The Moebius function: 0 if n has a squared prime factor, otherwise (-1)^k where k is the number of distinct prime factors. It is the kernel of Moebius inversion and appears throughout multiplicative number theory. Sums of MoebiusMu relate directly to the distribution of primes.
tools.example:
MoebiusMu[6]
MoebiusMu[12]
MoebiusMu[30]
Table[MoebiusMu[n], {n, 1, 12}]
Sum[MoebiusMu[d], {d, Divisors[10]}]

tools.name: PowerMod
tools.description: Computes a^b mod m efficiently by repeated squaring, without ever forming the huge intermediate power. A negative exponent gives the modular inverse of the corresponding power, and PowerMod[a, 1/r, m] computes modular roots. It is the core operation of RSA, Diffie-Hellman and primality testing.
tools.usage:
PowerMod[a, b, m]
PowerMod[a, -1, m]
PowerMod[a, 1/r, m]
tools.notes: Never write Mod[a^b, m] for large b: it computes the full power first and can exhaust memory. PowerMod is the only safe form.

tools.name: ModularInverse
tools.description: Gives the multiplicative inverse of a modulo m, i.e. the value x with a x == 1 mod m. It fails with a message when a and m are not coprime, since no inverse exists then. It is equivalent to PowerMod[a, -1, m] but reads more clearly.

tools.name: ChineseRemainder
tools.description: Solves a system of simultaneous congruences, returning the smallest non-negative x with x == r_i mod m_i for each i. The moduli need not be pairwise coprime; the function returns an answer only when the system is consistent. It is the standard tool for reassembling a result computed modulo several small primes.
tools.usage:
ChineseRemainder[{r1, r2, ...}, {m1, m2, ...}]
ChineseRemainder[rlist, mlist, d]

tools.name: ExtendedGCD
tools.description: Gives {g, {s, t, ...}} where g is the greatest common divisor and the second list holds the Bezout coefficients satisfying s a + t b == g. These coefficients are exactly what is needed for modular inverses and for solving linear Diophantine equations. It accepts any number of integer arguments.
tools.example:
ExtendedGCD[12, 18]
{g, {s, t}} = ExtendedGCD[17, 3120];
s * 17 + t * 3120
ExtendedGCD[6, 10, 15]

tools.name: ContinuedFraction
tools.description: Gives the continued fraction expansion of a number as a list of integer terms, with a nested list marking the periodic part for quadratic irrationals. A length argument limits how many terms are computed for irrational or approximate input. FromContinuedFraction reconstructs the value.

tools.name: Convergents
tools.description: Gives the list of rational convergents of a number or of a continued fraction list, i.e. the successive best rational approximations. Each convergent is the best rational approximation with a denominator no larger than its own. It is the standard route to good rational approximations of irrational constants.
tools.notes: 355/113 appears as the fourth convergent of Pi and is accurate to seven digits, which is why it is the classic approximation.

tools.name: IntegerPartitions
tools.description: Gives the list of ways to write an integer as a sum of positive integers, in reverse lexicographic order. A second argument bounds the number of parts and a third restricts which values may be used, which turns it into a general coin-change enumerator. The number of partitions alone is given far more cheaply by PartitionsP.
tools.usage:
IntegerPartitions[n]
IntegerPartitions[n, k]
IntegerPartitions[n, {k}]
IntegerPartitions[n, kspec, {s1, s2, ...}]
tools.example:
IntegerPartitions[5]
IntegerPartitions[6, 2]
IntegerPartitions[6, {3}]
IntegerPartitions[10, All, {1, 5, 10}]
Length[IntegerPartitions[20]]
tools.notes: The count grows subexponentially but fast: there are 190569292 partitions of 100, so always bound the enumeration or use PartitionsP.

tools.name: PartitionsP
tools.description: Gives the number of unrestricted integer partitions of n, computed by an efficient analytic method rather than by enumeration. PartitionsQ counts partitions into distinct parts. These are the standard counting functions in additive number theory.

tools.name: BellB
tools.description: The Bell numbers count the ways of partitioning a set of n labelled elements into non-empty subsets. The two-argument BellB[n, x] gives the Bell polynomials. Bell numbers appear when counting equivalence relations and set partitions.
tools.example:
BellB[4]
Table[BellB[n], {n, 0, 8}]
BellB[3, x]
Total[Table[StirlingS2[5, k], {k, 0, 5}]]
tools.notes: BellB[n] equals the sum over k of StirlingS2[n, k], which is a useful cross-check.

tools.name: StirlingS1
tools.description: The signed Stirling numbers of the first kind, the coefficients in the expansion of the falling factorial as a polynomial. Their absolute values count permutations of n elements with exactly m cycles. They convert between the ordinary power basis and the factorial basis.
tools.example:
StirlingS1[5, 2]
Table[StirlingS1[4, m], {m, 0, 4}]
Expand[Product[x - k, {k, 0, 3}]]
Abs[StirlingS1[5, 3]]

tools.name: StirlingS2
tools.description: The Stirling numbers of the second kind, counting the ways to partition a set of n labelled elements into exactly m non-empty unlabelled blocks. They convert from the power basis to the falling factorial basis, which makes them the key to summing powers. Their row sums are the Bell numbers.
tools.example:
StirlingS2[5, 2]
Table[StirlingS2[5, m], {m, 0, 5}]
Total[Table[StirlingS2[5, m], {m, 0, 5}]] == BellB[5]
StirlingS2[10, 3]

tools.name: CatalanNumber
tools.description: The Catalan numbers, counting balanced parenthesizations, binary trees, triangulations of a polygon and monotonic lattice paths that stay below the diagonal. CatalanNumber[n] equals Binomial[2n, n]/(n+1). They are one of the most frequently occurring sequences in combinatorics.

tools.name: Multinomial
tools.description: Gives the multinomial coefficient (n1 + n2 + ...)!/(n1! n2! ...), the number of ways to split a set into groups of the given sizes. It generalizes Binomial to more than two parts and gives the coefficients in the expansion of a multinomial power. All arguments may be symbolic.
tools.example:
Multinomial[2, 3]
Multinomial[1, 2, 3]
Multinomial[2, 3] == Binomial[5, 2]
Expand[(a + b + c)^3]

tools.name: Binomial
tools.description: The binomial coefficient n choose m, extended to non-integer and complex arguments through gamma functions. It is exact for integer input regardless of size and is Listable. Binomial is the basic counting function for combinations and the coefficient in the binomial expansion.
tools.example:
Binomial[5, 2]
Binomial[100, 50]
Binomial[n, 2] // FunctionExpand
Table[Binomial[4, k], {k, 0, 4}]
Binomial[1/2, 3]
tools.notes: Binomial[n, m] is 0 for integer n >= 0 and m > n, which makes sums over an unbounded range terminate automatically.

tools.name: Factorial
tools.description: The factorial n!, written with the postfix ! operator, exact for non-negative integers of any size and extended to other arguments through Gamma. Factorial of a negative integer is ComplexInfinity. For very large arguments in numeric work, use LogGamma instead to avoid overflow.
tools.notes: Wolfram Language integers are unbounded, so 10000! is computed exactly; it simply takes time and memory.

tools.name: Factorial2
tools.description: The double factorial n!!, the product of every other integer down from n, written with the postfix !! operator. For even n it gives the product of even numbers and for odd n the product of odd numbers. It appears in Gaussian moment formulas and in the normalization of spherical harmonics.

tools.name: Pochhammer
tools.description: The rising factorial (a)_n == a (a+1) ... (a+n-1), equal to Gamma[a+n]/Gamma[a]. It is the standard notation in the series definitions of hypergeometric functions and in the calculus of finite differences. FactorialPower gives the falling factorial instead.
tools.example:
Pochhammer[2, 3]
Pochhammer[a, 3] // Expand
Pochhammer[1, n]
FactorialPower[5, 3]
Sum[Pochhammer[a, k] z^k/k!, {k, 0, Infinity}]

tools.name: Fibonacci
tools.description: The Fibonacci numbers F_n, computed in logarithmic time by fast doubling so that Fibonacci[10^6] is immediate. The two-argument Fibonacci[n, x] gives the Fibonacci polynomials, and LucasL gives the companion Lucas sequence. Non-integer arguments are handled through the analytic continuation involving GoldenRatio.
tools.example:
Fibonacci[10]
Table[Fibonacci[n], {n, 1, 12}]
Fibonacci[1000]
LucasL[10]
Fibonacci[5, x]
tools.notes: N[Fibonacci[n+1]/Fibonacci[n]] converges to GoldenRatio; LinearRecurrence is the general tool for other constant-coefficient sequences.

tools.name: Subsets
tools.description: Generates the subsets of a list: all 2^n of them, or only those of specified sizes when a count specification is given. Subsets[list, {k}] enumerates exactly the k-element combinations, which is the standard combination generator. A fourth argument selects a range of subsets by index without generating the earlier ones.
tools.usage:
Subsets[list]
Subsets[list, n]
Subsets[list, {n}]
Subsets[list, {nmin, nmax}]
Subsets[list, nspec, {imin, imax}]
tools.example:
Subsets[{a, b, c}]
Subsets[Range[5], {2}]
Length[Subsets[Range[20], {3}]]
Subsets[Range[100], {2}, 5]
Subsets[{a, b, c}, {1, 2}]
tools.notes: The number of subsets grows exponentially; use the index-range form to enumerate lazily or Binomial to count without generating.

tools.name: Tuples
tools.description: Generates all ordered tuples, i.e. the Cartesian product. Tuples[list, n] gives all n-tuples drawn with repetition from a single list, and Tuples[{l1, l2, ...}] gives the product of several different lists. Results are in lexicographic order with the last position varying fastest.
tools.usage:
Tuples[list, n]
Tuples[{list1, list2, ...}]
Tuples[expr, n]
tools.notes: Outer keeps the nested array structure of the same combinations, which is often preferable for numerical work.

tools.name: Permutations
tools.description: Gives all distinct permutations of a list, or all arrangements of a given length. Repeated elements produce only distinct orderings, so Permutations[{1, 1, 2}] gives three results rather than six. Permutations[list, {k}] enumerates the ordered k-element arrangements.
tools.example:
Permutations[{a, b, c}]
Permutations[{1, 1, 2}]
Permutations[Range[4], {2}]
Length[Permutations[Range[6]]]
tools.notes: For large n use RandomSample for random permutations, and the Cycles/PermutationGroup functions for group-theoretic computation instead of explicit enumeration.

tools.name: KroneckerDelta
tools.description: Gives 1 when all its arguments are equal and 0 otherwise, the discrete analogue of the Dirac delta. With one argument it is 1 at zero and 0 elsewhere. It is used to write sums and tensor expressions compactly and simplifies automatically inside Sum.
tools.example:
KroneckerDelta[0]
KroneckerDelta[2, 2]
KroneckerDelta[1, 2]
Sum[KroneckerDelta[i, j] a[i], {i, 1, 5}]
Table[KroneckerDelta[i, j], {i, 3}, {j, 3}]

tools.name: DiracDelta
tools.description: The Dirac delta distribution, which is zero everywhere except at the origin and integrates to 1. It is handled symbolically: Integrate, LaplaceTransform and Convolve know its sifting property, and its derivatives DiracDelta' are also supported. It appears naturally in Green's functions and impulse responses.
tools.example:
Integrate[DiracDelta[x] f[x], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
Integrate[DiracDelta[x - 2] x^2, {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
LaplaceTransform[DiracDelta[t], t, s]
D[HeavisideTheta[x], x]
tools.notes: DiracDelta is a distribution, not a function: evaluating DiracDelta[0] gives an unevaluated expression, and it is only meaningful inside an integral.

tools.name: UnitStep
tools.description: The unit step function, 0 for negative arguments and 1 for non-negative ones, with several arguments giving the product of the individual steps. HeavisideTheta is the distributional version, left undefined at zero, which is the right choice inside integrals and derivatives. UnitStep is the practical choice for defining piecewise numeric functions.
tools.example:
UnitStep[-1]
UnitStep[0]
UnitStep[x] - UnitStep[x - 1]
Integrate[UnitStep[x] Exp[-x], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
Plot[UnitStep[x - 2], {x, 0, 4}]
tools.notes: Related shape functions include UnitBox, UnitTriangle, Ramp and Clip; Piecewise is the general construct for functions defined by cases.

tools.name: Boole
tools.description: Converts a logical expression into 1 when True and 0 when False, leaving it unevaluated otherwise. It turns conditions into arithmetic, which lets Integrate and Sum handle constraints as indicator functions and lets you count matches with Total. It is the standard bridge between boolean and numeric computation.
tools.example:
Boole[True]
Boole[3 > 2]
Boole[{True, False, True}]
Total[Boole[EvenQ /@ Range[10]]]
Integrate[Boole[x^2 + y^2 < 1], {x, -1, 1}, {y, -1, 1}]
tools.notes: Integrating Boole of a region condition is a standard way to compute areas and volumes of implicitly described regions.

tools.name: BitAnd
tools.description: Gives the bitwise AND of integers, treating them as two's-complement binary numbers of unbounded length. It is Listable and works on negative integers with the expected infinite sign extension. Use it for masking flags and extracting bit fields.

tools.name: BitOr
tools.description: Gives the bitwise OR of integers, again with unbounded two's-complement semantics. It is used to combine flag masks and set bits. BitNot gives the bitwise complement, equal to -n - 1.

tools.name: BitXor
tools.description: Gives the bitwise exclusive OR of integers. It is its own inverse, which makes it the basis of simple ciphers, checksums, hashing mixes and Nim-style game analysis. BitXor of a list of values under Apply computes the Nim sum of a position.

tools.name: BitShiftLeft
tools.description: Shifts the binary digits of an integer to the left by a given number of positions, equivalent to multiplying by a power of two. BitShiftRight shifts the other way, performing an arithmetic (sign-preserving) shift that rounds toward negative infinity. Related bit-level functions include BitLength, BitGet and BitSet.
tools.usage:
BitShiftLeft[n, k]
BitShiftRight[n, k]
BitLength[n]
BitGet[n, k]
